description:
Four would-be crew with a profession each and no class. No captain in Ashford signs on the unbound, so they take the only job that pays enough to bind four: a merchant's daughter, lost in the sewers under Refinery Row.

Act 1 of the Wayfinder story for the Possibilities system: your own character plus Enkrid, Rook and Tova, from the Coast Road to the day the Gilded Tern leaves without them. Seven maps, the Act 1 Director, the Purse, the Into the light Scene with its sun clock, and My Story, a journal for writing it up as you play.

Start with the Act 1: Ashford Roads journal, or the Act 1 Director (Shift+A).

Crow-kin from an old Bench family on the mainland, raised to copy charts and never draw one. Has seen every coastline in his father's archive once, so he can draw them all, and can do his father's voice well enough to sign for him. He left with one satchel, three stolen pens, and a debt of disappointment he means to outrun.

Motivation: To escape the mundane and cruel life of the mainland, building power and knowledge to feel free from family and cultural expectations.

Playing Act 1 on your own

Draft by Claude How-to text written for the module.

You are the GM and the player. You play {pc}, your own character, and you also run Enkrid, Rook and Tova, who follow the story's paths. Everything else (the broker, the rats, the Gloam) is yours to run as GM.

  1. Open the Act 1 Director (@Act1[openDirector]{Act 1 Director}, or Shift+A). It lists the 14 steps in order: read each scene aloud, open its page, show its map, and tick it off.
  2. Make your character first (@Act1[makeCharacter]{Make your character}). You pick race, profession, skills and looks. No class yet: everyone starts Unclassed, and the class is chosen at the Binding House.
  3. Roll in the open. Every check is d20 + modifier against a DC, and the chat card says what it means. Let the dice surprise you; that is what makes it a story rather than an outline.
  4. Write as you go. Each step has a page in My Story with a short prompt. "Write this beat" in the Director opens it. The Session log page collects what happened each time you stop (@Act1[sessionLog]{Write the session log}).
  5. Ask the oracle when you don't know what the world would do (@Act1[oracle]{Ask the oracle}): a yes/no question, likely / even / unlikely, and the answer comes back as Yes, and / Yes / Yes, but / No, but / No / No, and.
  6. Change anything. Pages marked Draft by Claude were drafted for you; your own canon is marked Your canon. Edit freely: the story is yours.

Money: the party needs 4 bindings at 50 gold crowns (gp) to be classed. The @Act1[openPurse]{Purse} tracks it.

When you're done, @Act1[copyStory]{Copy my story} turns My Story into clean text you can paste into Word.

Act 1: Ashford Roads

The home port. A deepwater harbour, a Compact refinery running day and night, a Bench office, and eleven thousand people who mostly work for one or the other. Everything a crew needs is here, at a price, and everything they do is noticed. Everyone but the Compact calls it Ashford.

From the story deck's events 01-05 ("But Then, Therefore"): the four meet at the broker, but they must be classed to join a ship; therefore the sewer job; they barely earn it; therefore they are bound, delayed, and miss the first ship.

The Reach, for Act 1

Draft by Claude The setting primer for Act 1. Draft by Claude, written from the user's answers on the Ashford Roads Decisions page (10 Nov 2026) and the lore. Replace any of it.

Two words: Dungeonpunk and gaslit

Dungeons in the Reach are made by industry: sewers, refinery works, flooded pump-halls, Compact-licensed ruins, wrecked brume engines. Delving is a trade, with brokers, permits, insurers and danger fees, and crews do it for the money.

It is a gaslamp-era society where the gas is refined brume: charge-lamps on every street, refinery smoke, licences and ledgers, top hats and soot, class lines you can see. Magic is an industry and a profession, not a mystery.

Grim streets, hopeful crew. The cruelty is systemic and the danger is real, but the story is about found family, wonder, and getting out. The banter stays: dry, quick, and never at the expense of a serious beat.

Brume is the power

Brume is a grey fog of unfixed Possibility lying on the open sea, and every kind of power in the world comes from it.

Bound into a person, it becomes their class and their grade: that is binding, and it is why the Binding House charges what it does. Refined, it becomes charge, sealed in glass cells that light the lamps and run the lifts, pumps and engines. Drawn on by the bound, it becomes spells and signatures.

Breathed in deep water, it slowly unwrites anything that isn't bound. That is why the sea outside the Reach eats the unclassed, and why no insurer will cover them.

Charge and sky ships

Charge cells are graded like everything else; a full F-grade cell costs about a day's wage. Night streets are pools of amber charge-light in grey fog.

Sky ships are new, about thirty years old, and rare because they take years to build. What makes them fly is the brume engine. Aurelio Fenn, the inventor, built the brume possibility engine; the legends' expedition was rumoured to fly on one. In Ashford a sky ship is a dream and a rumour: almost nobody has seen one.

Who runs the Reach

The Compact is a chartered trading company that became a government in all but name: the refinery, the licences, the insurance, the Wardens, the debt. Polite, legal and merciless. In Act 1 it is everywhere and never the villain on screen.

The Bench is the courts and record-keepers: charts, deeds, inheritances and contracts. Bench families are old money that holds the maps, and a chart isn't true until the Bench stamps it.

The Wrights are a faith of makers who teach that the world was wrought and that fixing things is holy. Their chapels keep the clocks and the schools; tinkers are often Wright-raised.

On the streets there are two forces: the city Watch, underpaid and answering to the Bench, and the Compact Wardens, well paid and answering to the refinery. The monsterkin surety bond is Compact policy that the Watch enforces.

The Compact underwrites every voyage out of Ashford. No policy, no berth, and no harbour will take you. That is the real reason class is a gate.

The edge of the map

Kelder's Wall is the edge of the charted Reach: a standing bank of brume that never lifts, graded far above anything in the Reach. Ships that go past it rarely come back. The legends went past it eight years ago.

Peoples of Ashford

Mostly Founding peoples (humans, dwarves, half-orcs), a big beastkin quarter by the fish market, few fae, and monsterkin only on the quay.

Fae are distrusted, not hated: people think they leak Possibility and bring bad luck aboard. Polite avoidance, higher prices, captains who have no berths. Binding hits fae harder.

Monsterkin are second-class by law: surety bonds, one inn, lower wages, written policy. Plenty of ordinary people are kind one to one; the system isn't.

Weather, light and coin

Fog rolls in off the brume every night and burns off by mid-morning everywhere except Refinery Row, which stays clear and warm.

The sheets count cp, sp, gp and pp; people in the Reach say copper bits, silver marks, gold crowns and platinum charters. Prices triple with every grade.

The scene

Inside Sallow's Exchange. Rook and Tova are already at the high desk; the player joins the queue behind them.

Odile Sallow A crow with a satchel full of somebody else's pens. No.
Rook They're my pens. Now.
Odile Sallow And a Trollblood who wants a berth on a ship. Dear heart, I can't even get you a bed.
Tova I sleep on deck. I'm first up and last down. Write that on whatever you write.
Odile Sallow And you, {pc}. Let me guess. Big plans, no class.
  • I'm here for a ship.
  • I'm here for work.
Odile Sallow Everyone is. Sit down, the three of you, and stop blocking my door.

The door bangs. Enkrid comes in out of breath, a pocket watch chain swinging.

Enkrid Ashford Roads. Is this where the legends' crews hire? Captain Isolde Varr's people?
Odile Sallow Captain Isolde Varr has been gone eight years, little road fae. And now there are four of you.
Odile Sallow Here is the part none of you will like. No captain in this harbour signs on unclassed crew. Not even for the galley. Get bound, then come back.
Tova How much is binding?
Odile Sallow More than you have. All four together, more than you have.
Rook Then we put it together.
Enkrid Together. Yes.
Odile Sallow You've known each other a minute and a half.
Tova Then it's a good minute and a half. Give us work. And answer questions.
Odile Sallow Oh, I'll answer your stupid, basic, and naive questions. Questions are free today. Tomorrow they're a silver each.

The scene

The broker's answers are in @UUID[JournalEntry.DP5HHmTPLvsk1VVZ]{Stupid, Basic, and Naive Questions}: show any of them to the table.

Q: What is a class?

What binding gives you. Brume possibility bound into your body, and with it the way you fight. Until you're bound you can swing a stick like anyone; after, you're a Vanguard, a Theorist, whatever you pay for.

Q: What is a profession?

What you do when nobody's trying to kill you. Anyone can learn one. It's how you earn, mend, chart and cook, and in a harbour it matters more than your class.

Q: What is grade?

How firmly a thing is written into the world. You're F, or you will be once you're bound. Water has a grade too. Sail into water above your grade and it will tell you so.

Q: Why won't ships take unclassed crew?

Because the sea outside the Reach is unfixed, and unfixed water eats the unbound. Insurers won't cover you. Captains won't carry what the insurers won't.

Q: Who runs Ashford?

The Compact owns the refinery, the licences and most of the captains. The Bench owns the charts. I own what everyone tells me.

Q: Where did the legends' crew go?

Out past Kelder's Wall, eight years ago, on the best-found ship that ever left this quay. Nobody's heard a word. That's the honest answer. The dishonest ones cost more.

Something in the big cistern. Lamps don't scare it. Light does.

SALLOW'S EXCHANGE. Loaned and not returned whole:

Four blades, bent and chipped: 20 gold crowns.

One charge lamp, mirror cracked: 6 gold crowns.

One pry bar, tooth marks: 4 gold crowns.

Total 30 gold crowns. Paid. The goods are now the borrowers' own.

Draft by Claude

THE COMPACT. Licensed Binding House, Ashford Roads.

Bindings at F-grade: four. Paid in cash. No debt recorded.

The Compact accepts no liability for discomfort, collapse, or what the bound do next.

Draft by Claude

A page in Captain Isolde Varr's hand, left with Old Dunmore against a bar tab eight years ago.

(Blank: this page is yours to write. Edit it here.)

Your canon

Everyone can learn a profession, but becoming classed means paying to have brume possibility bound into you. Unclassed is the tier at the bottom, before F. The heroes start Unclassed.

Your canon

Making Possibility permanent in a person, which is what produces grade. Licensed in Compact waters; licensed binding carries a debt to the Compact. In the game, binding is the paid step that gives a hero their class.

Your canon

The race family once listed as Monster. Monsterkin hate being lumped in with the mindless beasts and monsters of the world; they are no less enlightened than anyone, just with different challenges. "Monster" is what the Compact writes on the manifest.

Your canon

Crystal-faced and engraved: a token of identity and remembrance of Enkrid's goals. The inventor leaves it with him before the legends depart.
